document.abstract: A film transport system was designed and manufactured for the Fox Movietone News Preservation Project. It is a complete system designed to accommodate nitrate-base 35mm film. The film transport was designed with a number of unique features that presented significant technical challenges; among them, the ability to allow for film format differences between silent and sound film, a strobe illumination system for the high-resolution black-and-white charge-coupled device (CCD) camera, and a sound reader. The system also had to incorporate numerous safeguards in the design to secure the integrity of the film. For example, the system had to be concerned with the brittle nature of the film, its combustibility, and poor or broken perforations. Moreover, owing to the tremendous volume of film to be passed through the film transport, the design had to consider mechanical wear and electronic monitoring in order not to place undue stress over time on the film. Various technical approaches were evaluated for the design. The effort was complicated by the realization that the “best” approach might leave the film vulnerable. Thus, other avenues needed to be included even though they could add complexity and bulk. What evolved through this series of trade-offs is presented in this paper.

authors.bio: Julian E. Hansen is chief engineer, Mekel Engineering, Inc., where he is responsible for the technical and management aspects of its high-technology engineering processes. Hansen previously spent five years as chief engineer with Javelin Electronics, Torrance, Calif. Earlier he was vice-president, engineering, for Convergence Corp., Irvine, Calif., a videotape editing equipment manufacturer, where he extensively interfaced with the motion picture and television broadcasting industries. He previously was chief engineer for 17 years at Dynair Electronics, Inc., San Diego. — Hansen graduated from San Diego State University with a B.S. in physics/electronics and from West Coast University with an M.S. in computer science. He holds two patents.
authors.name: Julian E. Hansen

authors.bio: Daniel G. Lorti is vice-president and general manager, Mekel Engineering, Inc., Brea, Calif., a subsidiary of Metters Industries, Inc., McLean, Va. He previously spent ten years with Northrop Grumman Corp. as chief radar engineer, director of advanced systems, and director of business development. Prior to joining Northrop Grumman, Lorti was cofounder, vice-president, and director of the Advanced Systems Division of XonTech in Van Nuys, Calif. Earlier he held several posts with Xonic, Inc., Chicago, and Xonics Technology, Inc., Van Nuys. — Lorti holds B.S.E. and M.S.E. degrees in electrical engineering from Arizona State University, and subsequently did post-graduate work at the University of California at Irvine. He is the author of over 80 technical publications and holds three patents.
authors.name: Daniel C. Lorti

authors.bio: Roy W. Thrash is project engineer at Mekel Engineering, Inc., where he is responsible for the design and implementation of film and video cameras, film transports, and optical systems projects. Thrash has participated in the development of such advanced systems as the Eight Camera Sequencer Alpha Numeric Data System, Analog Data Formatter, and the Twentieth Century-Fox Movietone Automatic Film Transport. Previously he was the principal of Control Systems Specialties, Costa Mesa, Calif., and senior electronic engineer at Photographic Sciences, Santa Ana, where he developed a bar-code production system. — Thrash graduated from Citrus College with a degree in math and chemistry and also studied digital systems at Cal-Poly University and electronic engineering at West Coast University. While serving in the U.S. Navy he specialized in sonar electronics.
authors.name: Roy Thrash
